title: Elasticity
lede: Umberto Boccioni fuses a galloping horse and rider with an industrial landscape of pylons and factories, so that the bodies, the ground, and the buildings share one set of curving planes.
summary: A red horse and rider burst through planes of green fields, pylons, and factories. Umberto Boccioni, 1912.

source.label: Wikimedia Commons: Umberto Boccioni, 1912, Elasticity, Museo del Novecento

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Commons file (1100 × 1089 px; credited to the blog artblart, not to the museum). The physical work is the painting in the Museo del Novecento, Milan, Jucker Collection, according to [Italian Wikipedia](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elasticit%C3%A0_(Boccioni)) as summarized by a web search; that page was not opened directly. The museum’s inventory number was not checked.

styles.note: Plastic dynamism at its most developed: horse, rider, and industrial landscape interpenetrate in one field of planes and lines of force.

context: Oil on canvas, 100 × 100 cm, 1912, Museo del Novecento, Milan, Jucker Collection. The painting shows a rider at speed in an industrial landscape. [Italian Wikipedia: Elasticità (Boccioni)](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elasticit%C3%A0_(Boccioni)).

The Museo del Novecento has digitized the painting in gigapixel resolution. [Finestre sull’Arte](https://www.finestresullarte.info/musei/museo-del-novecento-milano-digitalizzati-tecnologia-gigapixel-capolavori-boccioni-modigliani-klee).
observed: A red and crimson horse fills the lower half, its legs and body drawn as stacked curved planes; a rider in ochre and brown sits above it.
A dark blue-black form at the center, possibly the horse’s head or a harness, is the only near-black area.
Behind and through the figures are green fields, red-roofed factories, smoking chimneys, and a lattice electricity pylon at upper right.
Thin straight black lines cross the lower left like struts or rays.
Pale yellow spirals and arcs at the bottom suggest dust or the curve of the gallop.
The palette is saturated and prismatic: red, crimson, violet, ochre, green, and blue, with small white highlights.
interpretation: *Elasticity* sits between [The City Rises](ref:boccioni-the-city-rises-1910) and [Dynamism of a Cyclist](ref:boccioni-dynamism-of-a-cyclist-1913): the horse is still present, but the forms are now planes that also belong to the surrounding landscape, so the animal and the machine age merge.
The pylon and chimneys keep the Futurist subject of the electrified, industrial city in a picture of a horse.
borrow: Let a moving subject share its planes with the background so that the boundary disappears at the points of greatest speed.
Use a square format filled edge to edge, with no calm margin.
Put one dark accent at the center of a hot palette to anchor the composition.

images.alt: Square painting of a red horse and an ochre rider made of curved, overlapping planes, bursting through a background of green fields, red-roofed factories, chimneys, and an electricity pylon. Black struts cross the lower left and pale yellow spirals fill the bottom.
images.caption: Umberto Boccioni, *Elasticity*, 1912, oil on canvas, 100 × 100 cm. Museo del Novecento, Milan. Image from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Umberto_Boccioni,_1912,_Elasticity_(Elasticit%C3%A0),_oil_on_canvas,_100_x_100_cm,_Museo_del_Novecento.jpg), marked public domain.

rights.statement: Wikimedia Commons marks the file public domain. Boccioni was Italian and died in 1916, so the painting is public domain in Italy. It dates from 1912 and its author died more than 70 years ago, so it is also public domain in the United States. The image is a faithful reproduction of a two-dimensional work.
